metadata.title: Claude, Form Generation.
metadata.subtitle: A Checklist, Not a Draft
metadata.purpose: Answer one real question in the Teardown register: did Claude design the legal form, or is it following a fixed checklist? Lands the carry-out that a skill is a file of fields Claude reads before it starts, not drafting talent.

beats.narration_text: Read 'form-generation skill' and you picture Claude drafting a legal form from a blank page. Not what's happening. The skill's a file of instructions Claude was handed. Let's open it. Liam, in for Bear.

beats.narration_text: Here's the natural read. 'Claude has a form-generation skill' sounds like a drafting upgrade — new muscle, blank page, out comes a legal document. That's what the phrase promises. Now watch what it actually is.

Run the test. Delete the skill's folder and Claude still writes fluent sentences — no drafting talent was stored there to lose. What breaks is the checklist: the specific fields that particular form needed, in the order it needed them. The prose was never the skill.

production_viz.label: NOTHING TO FORGET
production_viz.caption: there was no drafting talent stored there

beats.narration_text: Here's the actual machinery. A skill is one file. Form-generation is a folder holding a single SKILL.md — plain-language instructions naming which fields the form needs and where the case facts go. Claude reads that file before it starts. That's the whole apparatus.

Here's how it runs. Claude reads that file top to bottom and fills each field in the exact order it's listed — no branching, no re-arranging, unless the file itself says branch. The order in the file is the order in the output.

This makes a skill a specification, not talent. They optimized for uniform output at the expense of flexibility. The payoff: every form you get back has the same field layout, every time. The cost: any field the file never listed doesn't exist as far as Claude is concerned — no instructions for it, so no field.

So form-generation never taught Claude how to draft a legal document from nothing. What it guarantees is different: every run, same file, same fields, same order. That's the whole trick — and once you see it as a checklist rather than a talent, the naming stops misleading you.

shot.new_visual_element: THE ANCHOR RETURNS — SAME FILE, EVERY RUN

production_viz.label: THE ANCHOR RETURNS — SAME FILE, EVERY RUN
production_viz.caption: same file, same fields, every run

beats.narration_text: This cuts both ways. A cleanly filled form doesn't prove Claude understood the case — the checklist runs the same whether or not Claude parsed the underlying facts. And a wrong or empty field doesn't prove the skill is broken — it may be a case the checklist was never written to cover. They optimized for structural reliability, not for judgment about scope. Both signals send you back to the checklist itself, not to trust or blame the run.
A skill doesn't teach Claude to draft a legal document from nothing — it's a checklist of fields Claude reads before it starts, so every form comes out with the same structure, every time.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Paste this into Claude, ChatGPT, or Gemini: I want to turn one routine document I fill out the same way every time — an intake form, a client memo, an invoice, a status report, anything — into a reusable checklist so any capable AI can produce a consistent version of it. Ask me one clarifying question if you need to, then draft me a plain-language SKILL.md: a short description, then every field the document requires in the exact order it needs them, saying for each field where the input comes from and what happens when it's missing. Read it back to me and walk through what you'd fill in on a sample case before you fill anything in. Go deeper: take that same SKILL.md and tell me what edge cases it doesn't cover — the kinds of inputs that will silently produce a bad form because there's no field for them.
